'''''Erythrina crista-galli''''', also known as the '''cockspur coral tree''', '''ceibo''' (in Spanish) or '''corticeira''' (in Portuguese), is a species of flowering [[tree]] in the family [[Fabaceae]], native to Argentina, Uruguay, Bolivia, southern Brazil and Paraguay.  It is widely planted as a street or garden tree in other countries, notably in [[California]]. Its [[botanical name|specific epithet]] ''crista-galli'' means "[[comb (anatomy)|cock's comb]]" in Latin.

It is the [[List of national trees|national tree]] of Argentina, and its flower the [[Floral emblem|national flower]] of Argentina and Uruguay.

==Description==
[[File:Erythrina crista-galli flowers, 7th Brigade Park, Chermside IMGP6687.jpg|thumb|left|A tree blooming in [[Brisbane]], Australia]]
''Erythrina crista-galli'' is a small tree, the girth of its trunk measuring {{convert|50|cm|in|abbr=on}}. Normally it grows {{convert|5|-|8|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, although some individuals, such as in the Argentine provinces of [[Salta Province|Salta]], [[Jujuy Province|Jujuy]] and [[Tucumán Province|Tucumán]], can grow up to {{convert|10|m|ft|abbr=on}}. The woody trunk of the tree is equipped with irregular and [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|thorn]]y branches and can reach 50 cm in circumference.

The [[root]] is a [[taproot]] with [[root nodule|nodules]] produced by [[nitrogen-fixing]] bacteria. The bacteria live in [[symbiosis]] with the tree, facilitating the tree's absorption of nitrogen in return for organic substances which the bacteria need. The tree's trunk is woody with irregular, spiny branches. These branches form a layer without definite form<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.terrain.net.nz/friends-of-te-henui-group/tree-exotic-botanical-names-a-to-f/cockspur-coral-tree-erythrina-crista-galli.html|title=Erythrina crista-galli (Cockspur Coral Tree)|date=February 2015|website=Taranaki Educational Resource Research Analysis and Information Network}}</ref> and die after flowering.

===Flowers and fruit===
[[File:Erythrina crista-galli OB UJ Krakow 2017-09-28 5744.jpg|thumb|left|Flowers]]
[[File:Erythrina crista-galli 2-3.jpg|thumb|A tree in an urban park in [[Rosario]], [[Argentina]]]]
The red [[flower]], arranged in [[inflorescence]]s of the [[raceme]] type, is pentameric, complete, and of bilateral symmetry.  Its [[sepal|calyx]] is [[synsepal|gamosepalous]], like a little red thimble. The corolla, like that of other [[legume]]s like [[Phaseolus vulgaris|common bean]]s, is butterfly-shaped; however, the largest petal, called the "standard", is arranged in the lower part. The two petals called "wings" are so small that they are practically hidden within the calyx. The remaining two petals partially fuse together on occasion and form the flower's keel or "carina"; this protects its reproductive organs. The [[androecium]] consists of ten [[stamen]]s, one free and nine united by their filaments (gynostemial androecium). The unicarpel gynoecium is welded between the stamens like a knife in its sheath.

The tree flowers in the summer, from October to April in their native South America and from April to October in the northern hemisphere.

The flowers are rich in [[nectar]] and are visited by [[insect]]s, which usually have to crawl underneath the carina and thus [[pollination|pollinate]] the flowers.
[[File:Erythrina crista-galli MHNT.BOT.2007.52.19.jpg|thumb|Seeds]]

The tree's fruit is a [[legume]], a dry pod a few centimeters in length derived from a single [[carpel]] and contains about 8–10 chestnut-brown bean-shaped seeds. The cotyledons are [[hypogeal germination|hypogeal]], staying underground upon germination.

==Cultivation==
In cultivation in the United Kingdom this plant has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/32582/i-Erythrina-crista-galli-i/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder – ''Erythrina crista-galli''
| access-date=16 February 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants – Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 37 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 16 February 2018}}</ref> In urban settings, it is often planted in parks for its bright red flowers.

==Distribution==
It is distributed throughout northeastern and central western Argentina, eastern [[Bolivia]], [[southern Brazil]], much of [[Paraguay]], and almost all of Uruguay. It lives in low, flood-prone places, and along the watercourses of the [[Chaco Province|Chaco]] and the Eastern Region. It does not inhabit high forests or dry places without floods, as it tolerates water-saturated soils very well.

This species characteristically grows wild in [[gallery forest]] ecosystems along watercourses, as well as in swamps and wetlands.

It is naturalised in parts of Australia where it is a declared weed in some areas.<ref>{{cite web | title=Cockspur Coral Tree, Cockscomb Coral Tree, Coral Tree, Cockspur, Indian Coral Tree, Fireman's Cap, Crybabytree, Crybaby Tree | url=https://weeds.org.au/profiles/cockspur-coral-tree/ }}</ref>

==Uses==
It has [[dyeing]] and medicinal applications: its bark is used to treat [[rheumatism]] wounds and serves as a [[diuretic]] [[antispasmodic]]; its [[resin]] can cure intestinal diseases; Its leaves contain [[camphor]], that helps wound healing and has [[anti-inflammatory]] properties for tumors.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Metabolites from Endophytes of the Medicinal Plant Erythrina crista-galli|last1=Weber|first1=Daniela|last2=Gorzalczany|first2=Susana|date=1 June 2005|journal=Zeitschrift für Naturforschung C|volume=60|pages=467–477|issn=1865-7125|doi=10.1515/znc-2005-5-616|last3=Martino|first3=Virginia|last4=Acevedo|first4=Cristina|last5=Sterner|first5=Olov|last6=Anke|first6=Timm|issue=5–6 |pmid=16042349 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
